topics.speakEn: 4.11.4 Data Summarization and Statistical Analysis. Grouping combines rows that share a value (all CS students together) and then an aggregate calculates a number for the group. In Access click Totals (Σ) to reveal the Total row in the grid. Average marks per department: add Department and Marks; Totals Σ; Department → Group By; Marks → Avg; Run. Department Avg of Marks Computer Science 82.5 IT 76.0 Check: CS marks 80, 85 → average (80+85)/2 = 82.5. IT 70, 82 → 76.0. SELECT Department, AVG(Marks) AS AvgOfMarks FROM Student GROUP BY Department;

topics.titleUr: کمپیوٹنگ آج ہماری روزمرہ زندگی کا اہم حصہ بن چکی ہے۔ پاکستان میں اسکول…
topics.speakEn: 5.1 Introduction to Computing Impacts. Computing means using computers and computer-based devices to store, process and share information. Today computing is an important part of your daily life. You use computers, mobile phones, the internet and smart devices almost everywhere — at home, in college and on the road. In Pakistan, computing is becoming vital (very necessary) in: Schools and colleges — online admissions, e-books, online results of the Sindh boards. Hospitals — computerised patient records, digital X-rays, online appointment systems. Banks — ATMs, mobile banking apps, Raast instant payments, JazzCash and Easypaisa wallets. Farms — weather forecasts on mobile phones, soil sensors, tube-well control. Industries — automatic machines in textile mills in Karachi, Hyderabad and Faisalabad. An impact is the effect something has on people and society. Computing has positive impacts (speed, convenience, new jobs) and negative impacts (privacy risks, addiction, job loss). In this chapter you will study three key technologies first — AI, IoT and Data Analytics — and then their uses
topics.speakUr: کمپیوٹنگ آج ہماری روزمرہ زندگی کا اہم حصہ بن چکی ہے۔ پاکستان میں اسکول، اسپتال، بینک، کھیت اور صنعتیں سب کمپیوٹر اور انٹرنیٹ پر انحصار کرنے لگے ہیں۔ کمپیوٹنگ کے فائدے بھی ہیں اور نقصانات بھی، جنہیں ہم اس باب میں سمجھیں گے۔

topics.speakEn: 5.1.1 Artificial Intelligence (AI). Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the ability of a computer system to perform tasks that normally need human thinking, such as recognising faces, understanding language and making decisions. Understand the name in two parts: Artificial — it is created by humans ; it is not natural. Intelligence — it can perform tasks that require thinking . AI systems use data to make decisions . The more good data an AI system sees, the better it becomes at recognising patterns (repeating features) and predicting what to do. Examples from the source: Face recognition on a mobile phone to unlock the screen. YouTube suggesting videos based on your interests. Chatbots answering questions on a website (for example, a bank's help chat). More Pakistani examples: Google Maps predicting traffic on Shahrah-e-Faisal, Urdu voice typing on your phone, banks flagging a suspicious card transaction, and AI tools that translate English into Urdu. Smart air-conditioner in a hot Hyderabad room — trace the system: Step 1 (IoT – eyes). A temperature sensor reads the room temperature: 3

topics.speakEn: 5.1.2 Internet of Things (IoT) & Components. The Internet of Things (IoT) is a system in which physical devices are connected to the Internet and can collect and share data to perform tasks automatically . The "things" are ordinary objects — watches, cameras, cars, fans, water pumps — that have been given sensors and an internet connection so they can "talk" to each other and to us. Source example: A smartwatch collects your heart-rate data and sends it to your mobile phone, where it is displayed. Smart fire alarm in a Karachi factory — identify all six components: Step 1 — Sensor: A smoke sensor detects smoke near the machines. Step 2 — Connectivity: It sends the reading over the factory Wi-Fi. Step 3 — Cloud computing: The reading is stored on an online server along with the history of all sensors. Step 4 — Data processing: The software checks: "Is the smoke level above the safe limit?" Yes → decide "Fire risk!" Data Analytics is the bridge from data to information. Source example: A college collects exam marks, calculates percentages, and identifies which students need extra help. topics.speakEn: Comparison: IoT vs AI vs Data Analytics. These three technologies are often used together, so students mix them up. The table below, from the source, compares them on four aspects. One problem, three technologies — a K-Electric smart meter: IoT: The smart electricity meter measures units used every 15 minutes and sends them over the mobile network. Output: raw readings. Data Analytics: The company cleans and studies a month of readings and draws a graph showing that most electricity is used between 7 pm and 11 pm. Output: report/graph. AI: Software learns each area's pattern, predicts tomorrow's demand, and decides how to plan load management. Output: smart decision.

topics.speakEn: 5.2 Uses of IoT in Different Areas. IoT improves efficiency (doing more with less effort), saves time , and enhances the overall quality of life . It plays a significant role in developing modern infrastructure (the basic systems of a country — roads, power, water, hospitals). The source lists six areas. A cotton farmer near Nawabshah uses smart irrigation: Step 1. A soil moisture sensor in the field reads 18% moisture. Step 2. It sends the reading over the 4G network to a cloud service. Step 3. The cloud AI checks: cotton needs at least 25% moisture, and the weather forecast shows no rain → decision "Needs water: YES". Step 4. The actuator (pump switch) turns the tube-well ON. Step 5. When moisture reaches 30%, the AI decides "enough" and the pump turns OFF. Result: water is used only when needed — important because Sindh faces water shortages — and the farmer sees everything on his phone app.

topics.speakEn: 5.2.1 Scope of AI in Education in Pakistan. Artificial Intelligence is gradually becoming an important part of Pakistan's education system, improving teaching , learning and administration (managing the school: admissions, records, timetables). Practical uses: Learning Management Systems (LMS) — online platforms (e.g. Google Classroom, Moodle) where teachers post lessons and assignments; AI features can recommend lessons to each student. Automated grading and digital testing — MCQ tests marked instantly by computer. AI-based career counselling — software that studies a student's marks and interests and suggests suitable fields. Benefits: Helps students learn at their own speed . Identifies students who need extra help. Supports students with disabilities ( Assistive AI ), e.g. text-to-speech for a visually impaired student. Major challenges in Pakistan: Limited internet access in rural areas . Lack of computers and digital devices for all students. Need for proper teacher training to use AI tools. Data privacy and security issues — students' personal data must be protected. Scenario

topics.speakEn: 5.2.2 Career Connection in IoT and AI. Learning computing skills opens doors to many employers in Pakistan: software houses (e.g. in Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad technology parks), telecom companies (Jazz, Telenor), banks , and government IT departments (e.g. NADRA, provincial IT boards). IoT Engineer: designs smart systems and connected devices (e.g. a smart irrigation kit). Data Analyst: analyses the data generated by IoT systems and produces reports. Key skills needed: Programming — Python, C++. Networking — Wi-Fi, protocols (rules for how devices communicate). Electronics — sensors and circuits. Problem-solving .

topics.speakEn: 5.3 Information Sources (Primary, Secondary, Tertiary). Information sources are ways to find knowledge and data. The internet has vast information, but not all of it is accurate . Sources are divided into three main categories. 1. Primary sources give original, firsthand information straight from people, events or official records. They are highly authentic (genuine). Examples: interviews, photographs, diaries, NADRA official records. 2. Secondary sources contain information that has already been collected and explained by someone else . They summarise or analyse primary data . Examples: textbooks, news reports, research papers, Pakistan Bureau of Statistics reports. 3. Tertiary sources provide highly summarised and organised information derived from both primary and secondary sources. They are used for quick reference . Examples: encyclopedias, Wikipedia, dictionaries, handbooks. Classify these — worked solutions: (a) Your grandfather's handwritten diary from 1947. Written by a person who lived through the event → firsthand → Primary . (b) A Dawn newspaper article analysing the budg

topics.speakEn: 5.4 Impacts of Computing in Various Fields. Computing has drastically changed society. It makes life faster and more connected , but it also brings challenges like privacy risks and technology addiction . For every field, think of both sides. Scenario analysis — a bank in Karachi moves to mobile banking: Step 1 — Identify the field: Business (banking). Step 2 — Positive: Customers transfer money in seconds from home; no queue at the branch; the bank processes more transactions with fewer staff (speed and efficiency). Step 3 — Negative: Some cashier jobs are no longer needed (job loss); hackers may attempt cyber-attacks or phishing SMS to steal accounts. Step 4 — Responsible use: Customers should use strong passwords, never share OTPs, and report suspicious messages.

topics.speakEn: 5.5 Assistive Technologies. Assistive technologies are devices, software and systems that help people with disabilities or functional limitations (difficulty in seeing, hearing, moving, speaking, remembering, etc.). They allow more people to participate equally in school, work and society. There are four categories : Scenario — choose the right assistive technology: (a) Ahmed, a student in Hyderabad, is blind and wants to read his e-textbook. → Sensory aid : a screen reader or Braille display. (b) Mrs Rashida cannot climb the stairs of her house after a knee operation. → Mobility aid : stair lift (or smart wheelchair). (c) Zain cannot speak clearly due to a medical condition but can type. → Communication aid : text-to-speech app or speech-generating device. (d) Nani often forgets to take her medicine. → Cognitive aid : digital reminder app. (e) Usman has dyslexia (difficulty reading). → Cognitive/learning aid : audiobooks and spell-checkers. Method: identify the limitation (moving, seeing/hearing, speaking, memory/reading) → choose the matching category.
topics.speakUr: معاون ٹیکنالوجیز (Assistive Technologies) وہ آلات، سافٹ ویئر اور نظام ہیں جو معذور افراد کی مدد کرتے ہیں تاکہ وہ اسکول، کام اور معاشرے میں برابر حصہ لے سکیں۔ ان کی چار اقسام ہیں: نقل و حرکت میں مدد (اسمارٹ وہیل چیئر)، حسی مدد (سماعتی آلہ، اسکرین ریڈر، بریل ڈسپلے)، گفتگو میں مدد (اسپیچ جنریٹنگ ڈیوائس) اور ذہنی و تعلیمی مدد (آڈیو بکس، اسپیل چیکر، یاد دہانی ایپس)۔

topics.speakEn: 5.5.1 Importance of Assistive Technologies. Assistive technologies are important for three main reasons: Equal access to education: Screen readers allow blind students to read digital textbooks equally with their peers (classmates). Independence in daily life: Mobility aids reduce the need for constant human assistance — a person in a smart wheelchair can go to the market without someone pushing. Social inclusion: They break down barriers, allowing individuals to work, study and socialise confidently. How one tool changes a life: A visually impaired student in Karachi uses a screen reader on her laptop. Equal access — she reads the same e-books as her class. Independence — she no longer needs someone to read to her. Inclusion — she joins the class WhatsApp group, takes online tests and later gets a job, contributing to society.
topics.speakUr: معاون ٹیکنالوجیز کی اہمیت تین باتوں میں ہے: تعلیم تک برابر رسائی (نابینا طلبہ اسکرین ریڈر سے کتابیں پڑھ سکتے ہیں)، روزمرہ زندگی میں خود مختاری (کسی کی مسلسل مدد کی ضرورت کم ہوتی ہے)، اور سماجی شمولیت (لوگ اعتماد کے ساتھ پڑھ، کام اور میل جول کر سکتے ہیں)۔

topics.speakEn: 5.5.2 Career Connection in Assistive Tech. Designing assistive technology is a highly rewarding career path — you earn a living while improving people's lives. Career What they do Assistive Software Developer Creates tools such as speech-to-text software (e.g. Urdu voice typing for people who cannot use a keyboard). Biomedical Engineer Designs artificial limbs and hearing aids. UX/UI Accessibility Expert Ensures websites are easy to navigate for visually impaired users (e.g. adding text descriptions to images so screen readers can read them). UX means user experience (how easy and pleasant a product is to use); UI means user interface (the screens and buttons you interact with). Accessibility means designing so that everyone , including people with disabilities, can use it.

topics.titleUr: ڈیجیٹل خواندگی (Digital Literacy) سے مراد ڈیجیٹل آلات، انٹرنیٹ اور آن …
topics.speakEn: 6.1 Introduction to Digital Literacy. Digital literacy is the ability to understand and use digital devices, the internet, and online tools in a safe , effective , and responsible manner. Look at the three key words: Safe – you protect yourself and others online (for example, you do not share passwords or private details). Effective – you get the job done well (for example, you find the right information quickly). Responsible – you use information honestly and fairly (for example, you do not copy someone else's work or spread false news). In our increasingly digital world, digital literacy is essential for everyone , not only for computer experts. It enables you to: find information, communicate with others, produce digital content, and solve problems through technology. Is this student digitally literate? Ali can type fast and plays games on his phone all day. When his teacher asks him to find the population of Karachi, he copies the first number he sees on a random website and does not check where it came from. Step 1 – Can he use devices? Yes. He has basic skills. Step 2 – Can he
topics.speakUr: ڈیجیٹل خواندگی (Digital Literacy) سے مراد ڈیجیٹل آلات، انٹرنیٹ اور آن لائن ٹولز کو محفوظ، مؤثر اور ذمہ دارانہ طریقے سے سمجھنا اور استعمال کرنا ہے۔ ایک ڈیجیٹل خواندہ طالب علم معلومات تلاش کر سکتا ہے، انہیں ترتیب دے سکتا ہے، ان سے کوئی مفید چیز بنا سکتا ہے اور انہیں ذمہ داری سے دوسروں تک پہنچا سکتا ہے۔

topics.titleEn: 6.2 Digital Literacy in the Information Age
topics.titleUr: معلوماتی دور (Information Age) میں انٹرنیٹ اور موبائل کے ذریعے بے پناہ…
topics.speakEn: 6.2 Digital Literacy in the Information Age. The Information Age is the period we live in now, where vast amounts of data are produced , shared and accessed instantly through the internet, mobile devices and digital platforms (websites, apps, social media). Simply having access to technology is not enough . Owning a smartphone does not make you good at using information. You must develop the skills to understand , manage and use information wisely. Digital literacy goes beyond basic computer skills. It involves three kinds of ability: Ability What it means Example Technical Knowing how to operate devices and software. Creating a Google Form; using a spreadsheet. Cognitive (thinking) Thinking critically about information. Checking whether a news story is true before believing it. Social Communicating and behaving well with others online. Being polite in a class WhatsApp group; respecting privacy. Together these abilities help you function successfully in a digital society . Applying the three abilities. A video claims "Drinking hot water cures dengue." What does a digitally literate s
topics.speakUr: معلوماتی دور (Information Age) میں انٹرنیٹ اور موبائل کے ذریعے بے پناہ معلومات فوراً تیار اور شیئر ہوتی ہیں۔ صرف ٹیکنالوجی تک رسائی کافی نہیں؛ معلومات کو سمجھنے، سنبھالنے اور دانشمندی سے استعمال کرنے کی مہارت ضروری ہے۔ ڈیجیٹل خواندگی میں تکنیکی، ذہنی (Cognitive) اور سماجی صلاحیتیں شامل ہیں۔

topics.titleUr: کیفیتی ڈیٹا (Qualitative Data) الفاظ پر مشتمل ہوتا ہے اور بتاتا ہے کہ …
topics.speakEn: 6.3 Types of Data. Data means facts, numbers, words or observations that we collect. The data gathered through a survey, an investigation or a classroom project can be described in two ways: qualitatively or quantitatively . Knowing the difference is critical, because each type is analysed in a different way. Classify each piece of data. Data Type Reason "I like online classes because I can replay lectures." Qualitative An opinion with a reason, in words. Ayesha scored 78 out of 100. Quantitative A score – a number you can compare. 28 out of 40 students use the internet daily. Quantitative A count (and gives 70%). Observer notes: "Students chat during the last period." Qualitative A description of behaviour. Bilal spends 3.5 hours online per day. Quantitative A measurement of time. Quick test: ask "Can I calculate an average of this?" If yes, it is quantitative. If the answer is words, it is qualitative.

topics.speakEn: 6.4.1 – 6.4.2 Interviews and Surveys. An interview is a planned conversation used to gather information directly from a person . It may be one-to-one (you and one person) or in a small group . Questions are planned in advance , so you do not forget anything important. Answers are usually qualitative (opinions, reasons, experiences). Strength: you get deep, detailed answers and can ask follow-up questions ("Why do you say that?"). Weakness: it takes a lot of time, so you can only interview a few people. Building a short Google Form, step by step. Research question: "How do Class XI students travel to college?" topics.speakEn: 6.4.3 – 6.4.5 Prototypes, Observation and Simulations. A prototype is a simple early version of a product, model or solution. It allows an idea to be tested before time and effort are spent on the final version. Users try the prototype and give feedback , and this feedback becomes useful data for improvement . Example: Before building a full school app, you draw the screens on paper (or make a few clickable screens in a design tool) and ask five classmates to try "finding the timetable". You note where they get confused. Choosing the right method. Which method would you use? (a) "How many cars cross an intersection at 8 AM?" → Observation. Stand at the corner from 8:00 to 8:15 and tally each car. Asking drivers would be impossible and unnecessary; you just count. (b) "How do students feel about the new cafeteria food?" → Survey or interview. Feelings are inside people's heads, so you must ask them. Use a survey for many students, or interviews for deeper reasons. (c) "Will a new college website menu be easy to use?" → Prototype. Build a rough version and let users try it. (d) "What h

topics.speakEn: 6.5 Primary and Secondary Data. Whenever you use data, it is important to know where it came from . The source affects how much control the researcher had over collecting it, and how confidently the results can be used. Primary or secondary? Hira is researching "Internet use among students in Hyderabad". (a) She sends a Google Form to 50 students in her college. → Primary (she collected it herself, for this study). (b) She uses a PTA (Pakistan Telecommunication Authority) report on the number of broadband users in Pakistan. → Secondary (PTA collected it for its own purpose; Hira reuses it). (c) She counts how many students use phones in the library during one hour. → Primary (her own observation). (d) She quotes a statistic from a research article. → Secondary. Why use both? Her primary data tells her about her own college; the secondary data lets her compare it with the national picture.
topics.speakUr: بنیادی ڈیٹا (Primary Data) محقق خود کسی خاص مقصد کے لیے براہِ راست جمع کرتا ہے، مثلاً سروے، انٹرویو یا مشاہدہ۔ ثانوی ڈیٹا (Secondary Data) پہلے ہی کسی اور نے جمع کیا ہوتا ہے اور اسے نئے مقصد کے لیے دوبارہ استعمال کیا جاتا ہے، جیسے کتابیں، رپورٹس اور آن لائن ڈیٹا بیس۔ بنیادی ڈیٹا پر محقق کا کنٹرول زیادہ اور ثانوی ڈیٹا پر کم ہوتا ہے۔

topics.speakEn: 6.6 Designing a Data-Collection Approach. Before collecting data, a researcher must have a plan . A plan makes sure that the information gathered is accurate , relevant (related to the question) and useful . Follow these eight steps in order: Define the research question clearly. What exactly do you want to find out? Decide the type of data needed: quantitative, qualitative, or both. Select suitable methods (survey, interview, observation). Choose the sample or target group – the people who will give you data. Prepare the tools such as forms, questions and observation sheets. Collect the data carefully and accurately. Store the data digitally in a spreadsheet and keep a backup . Follow ethical practice and respect privacy. Consent is mandatory (you must get permission). Applying the eight steps. Topic: water wastage in your college. 1. Question: "How much water is wasted at the college taps during break time, and why?" 2. topics.speakEn: 6.7 Presenting Data Using Digital Tools: 6.7.1 Spreadsheets and 6.7.2 Presentations. Collecting data is only one part of the work. You must also present your findings so that others can understand them quickly and easily . Digital tools make this much easier. topics.speakEn: 6.7.3 – 6.7.4 Infographics and Reports. An infographic (information + graphic) is a visual way of presenting information, facts or data so that people can understand the main idea quickly and easily . Tools such as Canva , Power BI or Tableau can be used. A good infographic should: Simplify complex concepts. Highlight the most important findings and results. Use clear visuals , limited text and accurate information. Which tool should you choose? Situation Best tool Why You must calculate the average marks of 40 students. Spreadsheet Formulas calculate instantly. You will explain results to the class in assembly. Presentation Designed for a live audience. You want a one-page poster for the notice board. Infographic Main result understood at a glance. The principal wants the full study with method and recommendations. Report Detailed, structured document.

"academic performance" filetype:pdf filetype: Finds only PDF documents (often official reports and research papers). digital distraction site:.edu site: Searches only educational websites (addresses ending in .edu). topics.speakEn: 6.8 Steps 4 – 6: Survey Preparation and Primary Data Collection. Design clear, unbiased questions. Each question is linked to the type of data it produces: Question Type of data How many hours do you use your phone daily? Quantitative Which activity do you use your phone for the most? Quantitative (categories) How does your phone help you in studies? Qualitative Suggest one way to use phones responsibly. Qualitative Why "different sections" matters. Suppose the group surveyed only the 40 students of the Pre-Engineering section who sit in the front rows. Problem: these students might study more than average, so the results would show less phone distraction than is true for the whole class. Fix: pick students from every section (e.g. 10 each from Pre-Medical, Pre-Engineering, Computer Science and Commerce). Now the sample better represents all Class XI students. topics.speakEn: 6.8 Steps 10 – 12: Data Analysis, Conclusion and Recommendations. To analyse means to study the data carefully to find patterns and trends . By looking at the spreadsheet and charts, the group identifies: Most students (the majority) use phones for 3–5 hours daily . Half use it for educational purposes (lectures/notes). A clear trend: students who use phones mostly for entertainment report much higher distraction levels than those who use them for study. From numbers to a finding. Step 2: "Half use it for educational purposes" means about 20 of the 40 students chose Lectures or Notes as their main activity (20 ÷ 40 = 50%). Formula: =COUNTIF(D2:D41,"Lectures")+COUNTIF(D2:D41,"Notes") . Students must create one final artefact that answers the original research question. It is not just a decorated file ; it must present evidence and conclusions . Artefact option Suitable digital tools Main purpose Digital Report MS Word, Google Docs Explain the full study in a structured text document. Presentation PowerPoint, Canva, Slides Share key findings with a live audience. Infographic Canva, Adobe Express Show the main results visually and quickly on one page. Dashboard Power BI, Tableau Explore data through interactive charts and filters. Slide 3 Introduction: why the class investigated this. Slide 4 Method: Google Form survey, 40 students, different sections

topics.titleUr: ہیومن کمپیوٹر انٹریکشن (HCI) کا مطلب ہے ٹیکنالوجی کو اس طرح ڈیزائن کرن…
topics.speakEn: 1.1 Fundamentals of Human-Computer Interaction. Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) is the study and design of technology so that it serves people . An HCI system is easy to use, efficient, and responsive to human needs. HCI is also known as CHI (Computer-Human Interface) or MMI (Man-Machine Interaction). The three names mean the same idea: the meeting point of a person and a machine. HCI is not only "making a pretty screen". It asks: Can a student in Hyderabad find results on the school portal in 30 seconds? Can a grandmother send JazzCash without help? Can a person standing at an outdoor ATM in bright sunlight read the buttons? Worked example: map a JazzCash payment to channels. Sara in Sukkur sends Rs 500 to her brother. Sight: she looks at the JazzCash home screen and the amount field. Touch: she taps "Send Money" and types the mobile number. Voice (optional): she could say "JazzCash, send five hundred rupees" if voice commands are on. Hearing + haptics: a beep and a short vibration confirm "Payment successful". If the app showed no tick, no sound and no vibration, Sara would not kn
topics.speakUr: ہیومن کمپیوٹر انٹریکشن (HCI) کا مطلب ہے ٹیکنالوجی کو اس طرح ڈیزائن کرنا کہ وہ انسانوں کے لیے فائدہ مند، آسان اور مؤثر ہو۔ اسے CHI یا MMI بھی کہتے ہیں۔ انسان اور کمپیوٹر پانچ حسّی راستوں سے بات کرتے ہیں: بصارت، چھونا، سننا، آواز اور مکانی حرکت۔ ہیپٹکس (Haptics) وہ ارتعاش ہے جو آپ کو چھو کر محسوس ہوتا ہے۔

topics.titleUr: روایتی تعامل (Traditional Interaction) میں ماؤس، کی بورڈ، کی پیڈ یا عا…
topics.speakEn: 1.1.1 Traditional Interaction and 1.1.2 Natural Interaction. 1.1.1 Traditional interaction is the basic way people use everyday devices. It relies on standard input and output: a mouse, a keyboard, a keypad, a monitor, speakers, or a simple touchscreen tap and swipe. Computer: moving a mouse and typing on a keyboard; output via monitor and speakers. Smartphone (traditional use): tapping and swiping on a touchscreen; output via screen lighting and vibrations. 1.1.2 Natural interaction is advanced, smart technology that lets people interact without a mouse or keyboard . It feels more human — you speak, move, or show your face, and the system understands. Voice: speaking commands into a device (for example, "Alexa, play a song"). Body and gesture: facial recognition to unlock a phone, or playing VR games by waving hands. Worked example: sort today's tools. List three traditional and three natural interfaces you might use in one day in Sindh. Traditional: (1) HBL ATM keypad to withdraw cash. (2) College computer lab: mouse + keyboard to open the school portal. (3) Television remote at ho
topics.speakUr: روایتی تعامل (Traditional Interaction) میں ماؤس، کی بورڈ، کی پیڈ یا عام ٹیپ اور سوائپ استعمال ہوتے ہیں، جیسے اے ٹی ایم کی پیڈ۔ قدرتی تعامل (Natural Interaction) میں آواز، چہرہ یا جسم کی حرکت سے کام ہوتا ہے، جیسے فیس آئی ڈی (FaceID) یا "الیکسا، گانا چلاؤ"۔ درجہ بندی آلے کی نہیں، تعامل کے طریقے کی ہوتی ہے۔

topics.titleUr: ایچ سی آئی کی ایپلیکیشنز صحت، بینکنگ، تعلیم اور نیٹ ورکنگ کے شعبوں میں…
topics.speakEn: 1.2 Applications of HCI (Domains of Life). HCI is used to design and develop interactive systems such as desktop applications, websites and mobile apps . These are human-centred solutions built to meet user needs across many domains of life. A domain is an area of daily activity — health, money, school, talking to people. When you design for a domain, you design for that domain's users, tasks and risks . A mistake on a games app is annoying. A mistake on a medical or banking screen can harm a person or lose money. That is why examiners treat this topic as golden. Worked example: the same HCI idea in three Pakistani systems. Step 1 — ATM (banking). You insert a card, the screen shows large buttons (Fast Cash, Balance, Other), you enter a PIN on the keypad, and you take cash. HCI benefit: a quick, secure transaction without a human teller. Step 2 — JazzCash (banking + communication). You log in with a PIN or fingerprint, choose Send Money, type a number and amount, confirm, and see "Successful" with a JazzCash SMS. HCI benefit: money moves in seconds from a shop in Larkana to a student
topics.speakUr: ایچ سی آئی کی ایپلیکیشنز صحت، بینکنگ، تعلیم اور نیٹ ورکنگ کے شعبوں میں انسانی ضروریات پوری کرتی ہیں۔ صحت میں مریض پورٹل اور ٹیلی میڈیسن دور سے علاج دیتے ہیں، بینکنگ میں موبائل ایپ اور اے ٹی ایم تیز اور محفوظ لین دین دیتے ہیں، تعلیم میں ای لرننگ اور آن لائن امتحان مشغولیت بڑھاتے ہیں، اور واٹس ایپ یا زوم لوگوں کو جوڑتے ہیں۔

topics.titleUr: ایچ سی آئی کے چار بنیادی اجزاء ہیں: صارف (اینڈ یوزر جو خود سسٹم چلاتا …
topics.speakEn: 1.3 Components of HCI. HCI relies on several primary components that work together. If one component is weak, the whole interaction feels broken. The first four are the people, the machine, the conversation, and the job to be done. Worked example: label the four components of an HBL ATM withdrawal. User: end user = the account holder standing at the machine; stakeholder = the bank that owns the ATM and must keep it safe and working. Computer system: the ATM hardware plus the bank's software; it takes PIN input, shows a screen, and dispenses notes (output and feedback). User interaction: insert card → type PIN → choose "Cash" → type amount → confirm. Intent ("I want Rs 5,000") becomes a machine response (cash + receipt). Task: withdraw cash. Complexity: low (a few buttons). User knowledge: basic (PIN and amounts). Time: about one minute — much shorter than an online passport application.
topics.speakUr: ایچ سی آئی کے چار بنیادی اجزاء ہیں: صارف (اینڈ یوزر جو خود سسٹم چلاتا ہے اور اسٹیک ہولڈر جس کا نتیجے میں مفاد ہے)، کمپیوٹر سسٹم (ان پٹ، آؤٹ پٹ اور فیڈبیک کا پلیٹ فارم)، صارف کا تعامل (کلک، ٹیپ، ٹائپ، بولنا) اور کام (ٹاسک) جس کی پیچیدگی، مطلوبہ مہارت اور وقت مختلف ہوتا ہے۔ اے ٹی ایم سے رقم نکالنا آسان اور مختصر کام ہے؛ پاسپورٹ کی آن لائن درخواست لمبا کام ہے۔

topics.titleUr: تعامل کی اقسام میں براہِ راست ہیرا پھیری، کمانڈ، مینو، فارم، گفتگو (چی…
topics.speakEn: Types of User Interaction. User interaction can happen in many different ways depending on the technology used. Learn every type with one clean example — board questions often ask you to "list and explain" five or more. Worked example: a full JazzCash "Send Money" session, labelled by type. Open the app with a fingerprint → biometric . Home screen shows Send Money, Bill Payment, Load → you tap Send Money → menu-driven . Type the receiver's mobile number and the amount → form fill . The keypad vibrates on each tap → haptic . Optional: say "Send five hundred to Ali" then tap Confirm → multimodal (voice + touch). Same idea on a school portal : menu-driven ("Date Sheet", "Fee Challan"), form fill (leave application), conversational (a chatbot "When is the chemistry practical?").
topics.speakUr: تعامل کی اقسام میں براہِ راست ہیرا پھیری، کمانڈ، مینو، فارم، گفتگو (چیٹ بوٹ)، اشارہ، آواز، سیاق و سباق سے آگاہ نظام، بایومیٹرک، ہیپٹک اور ملٹی موڈل شامل ہیں۔ جاز کیش میں فنگر پرنٹ بایومیٹرک ہے، "رقم بھیجیں" مینو ہے، نمبر لکھنا فارم ہے، اور آواز کے ساتھ ٹیپ ملٹی موڈل ہے۔

topics.titleUr: یوزر انٹرفیس وہ واسطہ ہے جس سے انسان سسٹم سے بات کرتا ہے: GUI تصاویر ا…
topics.speakEn: Interface Types, Environment and Feedback. Components v–vii complete the HCI picture: the look of the controls, the place where you use them, and the signals that tell you "it worked" or "try again". v) User interface (UI) The user interface is the medium through which humans interact with computer systems. Graphical User Interface (GUI): visual elements such as windows, icons and menus (Windows OS, Android). Command-Line Interface (CLI): text-based typing (MS-DOS, Linux terminal). Touch interface: tapping, swiping, pinching (smartphones, tablets). Voice User Interface (VUI): spoken commands (smart speakers). Natural User Interface (NUI): gestures, body movements or immersive environments (VR headsets, Microsoft Kinect). vi) Environment The environment is the real-world setting where a person uses a computer system. It is shaped by: Physical conditions — an ATM outdoors in sunlight, heat, noise, rain. Social conditions — a quiet classroom, a crowded bazaar, privacy at a PIN pad. Technical hardware — slow college Wi-Fi, a cracked phone screen, an old browser. vii) Feedback Feedback is
topics.speakUr: یوزر انٹرفیس وہ واسطہ ہے جس سے انسان سسٹم سے بات کرتا ہے: GUI تصاویر اور مینو، CLI لکھی کمانڈ، ٹچ، آواز (VUI) اور قدرتی اشارے (NUI)۔ ماحول وہ حقیقی جگہ ہے جہاں سسٹم استعمال ہوتا ہے — دھوپ میں اے ٹی ایم، خاموش کلاس روم، کمزور وائی فائی۔ سسٹم فیڈبیک مشین کا جواب ہے ("بھیج دیا گیا")؛ صارف کا فیڈبیک صارف کا ان پٹ ہے (سبمٹ بٹن یا پانچ ستارے)۔

topics.titleUr: اچھا ایچ سی آئی پیچیدہ ٹیکنالوجی کو روزمرہ کا آسان اوزار بناتا ہے؛ برا…
topics.speakEn: 1.4 Importance of HCI. HCI ensures that machines are approachable and usable, turning complex technology into everyday tools. Good design makes technology simple and enjoyable (touchscreens). Poor design causes confusion and risks (unclear buttons on medical devices). This is why HCI is not optional decoration. A confusing JazzCash confirm button can send money to the wrong number. A confusing school-portal "Submit" can lock a student out of an online exam. Importance questions in the board exam expect the five implications below, each with a sentence of explanation. Worked example: good vs poor HCI, same task. Task: send Rs 2,000 through JazzCash to a parent. Good HCI: large "Send Money" button, amount shown in words and numbers, last 4 digits of the number repeated, fingerprint confirm, green "Successful" plus SMS. Result: fast, few mistakes, the user trusts the app (productivity + economic loyalty + ethics of clear consent). Poor HCI: tiny grey buttons, no amount-in-words, no confirm screen, no tick. Result: wrong number, no idea if it worked, user deletes the app and goes back to
topics.speakUr: اچھا ایچ سی آئی پیچیدہ ٹیکنالوجی کو روزمرہ کا آسان اوزار بناتا ہے؛ برا ڈیزائن الجھن اور خطرہ پیدا کرتا ہے، جیسے طبی آلے پر غیر واضح بٹن۔ پانچ مضمرات: پیداوری بڑھتی ہے، شمولیت آتی ہے، جدت اپنائی جاتی ہے، معیشت مضبوط ہوتی ہے، اور رازداری و انصاف کی اخلاقی ذمہ داری پوری ہوتی ہے۔

topics.titleUr: رسائی پذیری (Accessibility) کے اصول یقینی بناتے ہیں کہ ہر انسان سسٹم ا…
topics.speakEn: 1.5 Accessibility Principles. Accessibility principles are HCI guidelines that ensure digital systems are usable by all individuals, including people with diverse physical, sensory and cognitive abilities. They remove barriers to create equal access. Accessibility is not a "special extra". It is how you make sure a student with low vision, a shopkeeper who cannot use a mouse, or a colour-blind driver can still complete the task. Worked example: audit a school portal against the five principles. Contrast: are result PDFs pale grey on white? Fail — use dark text. Fonts: is the fee-challan note in 9-point decorative script? Fail — large Calibri (or a similar simple font), as the source recommends. Colour: is "fail" only a red row with no word "Fail"? Fail — add the word, for colour-blind students. Navigation: can a student who cannot use a mouse reach "Download date sheet" with Tab + Enter? If not, fail. Multimodal: does the principal's video assembly have captions, and does a fee-due alert vibrate as well as flash? If not, deaf or busy students miss it. The same five checks apply to an
topics.speakUr: رسائی پذیری (Accessibility) کے اصول یقینی بناتے ہیں کہ ہر انسان سسٹم استعمال کر سکے، بشمول مختلف جسمانی، حسّی اور ذہنی صلاحیتوں والے افراد۔ پانچ اصول: اونچا تضاد (کنٹراسٹ)، پڑھنے میں آسان فونٹ، صرف رنگ پر انحصار نہ کرنا، کی بورڈ سمیت متبادل نیویگیشن، اور معلومات کو نظر، آواز اور لمس کئی شکلوں میں دینا۔

topics.titleUr: نیڈ اینالیسس موجودہ صورتحال اور مطلوبہ نتیجے کے فرق کو یو آئی بنانے سے…
topics.speakEn: 1.6 Need Analysis for Interface Design. Need analysis is the process of identifying the gap between the existing situation and the desired outcome . In HCI it is done before designing a UI, so that you understand users' goals, tasks, abilities and expectations. If you skip need analysis, you guess. Guessing is how a school portal ends up with 40 menus and no "Download date sheet" button on the home screen. Case study from the source: mobile banking app. Before building the app, the team interviews customers and discovers: Users want secure login via Fingerprint / FaceID. Elderly users need large buttons and simple navigation. Users want support for both English and local languages. Result: the UI is designed around these proven needs, which makes success more likely. Apply the five steps to a college portal in Sindh. Users: Grade XI–XII students, parents, clerks, teachers. Not "everyone in Pakistan". Collect: interview 20 students; questionnaire to parents; watch a queue at the office on fee day. Analyse: students cannot find date sheets; parents cannot read English-only fee notices;
topics.speakUr: نیڈ اینالیسس موجودہ صورتحال اور مطلوبہ نتیجے کے فرق کو یو آئی بنانے سے پہلے تلاش کرتا ہے۔ پانچ قدم: صارفین کی پہچان، انٹرویو یا مشاہدے سے معلومات، ضروریات کا تجزیہ، اہم خصوصیات کو ترجیح، پھر تصدیق شدہ ضرورتوں پر حل۔ موبائل بینکنگ کی مثال: فنگر پرنٹ لاگ اِن، بڑے بٹن، اور انگریزی کے ساتھ مقامی زبان۔

topics.titleUr: ایچ سی آئی مسائل وہ رکاوٹیں ہیں جو سسٹم کو انسانی ضرورت یا ذہنی حد کے …
topics.speakEn: 1.7 Human-Computer Interaction Problems. HCI problems are common difficulties that stop users from using technology smoothly. They happen when systems fail to meet human needs or cognitive limits. Cognitive limits means the mind can only hold and process so much at once — if an app asks you to remember three SMS codes at the same time, it has gone past that limit. Board answers score well when you name the problem, explain it in one line, and give a concrete example (the source examples are safe; a matching local example is even better). Worked example: diagnose three local systems. ATM: six tiny unmarked buttons beside the screen and no "Cash is coming" message → interface complexity + poor feedback. A user walks away while cash is still coming out. JazzCash: "Send" is green on the home screen but orange on the confirm screen, and there is no padlock on the payment page → inconsistency + trust deficiency. School portal: works in Chrome on a lab PC, blank on a student's Android browser; exam instructions are a caption-free video; login needs a portal password, an email OTP and an SMS

topics.speakEn: 1.8 Methods for Improving HCI. Once you can name an HCI problem, you fix it with a matching method. The source lists eight methods. Learn each with its tiny example — they pair almost one-to-one with Section 1.7. Enhance usability: simplify navigation (a clear "Buy Now" button). Strengthen accessibility: support disabilities (captions on videos). Ensure consistency: keep layouts uniform (the same "Save" button everywhere). Provide clear feedback: show action results ("Payment Successful" popup). Improve adaptability: responsive design (the website scales to mobile screens). Apply user-centred design (UCD): focus on real user goals and pilot-test. Use multimodal interaction: allow touch, voice or gesture inputs combined. Continuous testing: regularly update based on user feedback. User-centred design (UCD) means the real user's goals drive every decision, and you trial (pilot-test) the design with those users instead of guessing in an office. Responsive design means the layout rearranges itself for phone, tablet and PC, instead of staying a laptop-only page. Worked example: match each

topics.speakEn: 1.9 User Interface Design (UI vs UX). UI design is the process of creating and organizing the visual elements of a software application so users can interact with it easily and efficiently. 1.9.1 Components of a user interface Component Role Buttons Clickable elements that perform actions (Submit, Cancel). Menus Lists of options for navigating the system. Icons Small symbols representing tools or actions. Text fields Boxes where users type information (passwords, search). Checkboxes / radio buttons Selecting options in a form. Checkboxes allow several choices; radio buttons allow only one in a group. Sliders Adjusting values along a bar (volume, brightness). 1.9.2 User experience (UX) UX is the overall experience a user has while interacting with a system — how smooth, comfortable and satisfying it feels. UI is what you see; UX is how it feels. Source example: food-delivery app. The UI is the nice pictures of burgers and the red buttons. The UX is that the app loads fast, tracking works, and the food arrives without the user getting frustrated. Local walk-through: JazzCash. UI: green
topics.speakUr: یو آئی ڈیزائن بصری عناصر — بٹن، مینو، آئیکن، ٹیکسٹ فیلڈ، چیک باکس/ریڈیو، سلائیڈر — کو ترتیب دینا ہے۔ یو ایکس پورا تجربہ ہے: کتنا ہموار، آرام دہ اور اطمینان بخش لگا۔ یو آئی وہ ہے جو آپ دیکھتے ہیں؛ یو ایکس وہ ہے جو آپ محسوس کرتے ہیں۔ کھانے کی ڈیلیوری ایپ میں برگر کی خوبصورت تصویر یو آئی ہے، تیز لوڈنگ اور وقت پر کھانا یو ایکس ہے۔

topics.speakEn: 1.9.3–1.9.5 Wireframing, Figma and Prototypes. 1.9.3 Wireframing is creating a basic visual outline or blueprint of a user interface before the final design. It plans the structure without focusing on colours or detailed graphics. Low-fidelity wireframes (Lo-Fi) A simple black-and-white sketch showing basic layout (boxes and lines). Used early to test and share ideas quickly. Focuses purely on structure and flow. Worked example: JazzCash-style "Send Money" in Figma, without writing code. Lo-Fi on paper or in Figma: three frames — Home (boxes: Send, Bills, Load), Amount (text field + Next), Success (tick + Done). Show the sketch to two classmates. If they cannot find Send, move that box to the top. This is the point of Lo-Fi: cheap changes. In Figma, add a phone frame, rectangles, and labels. Duplicate the frame for Home, Amount and Success. Prototype tab: Trigger = On Tap of the Send rectangle; Action = Navigate to Amount. On Tap of Next → Success. Hand the laptop to a student. If they tap Bills by mistake, the navigation is still wrong — fix it before any programmer writes Java or K

topics.speakEn: 1.11 Test and Evaluate HCI (Evaluation Methods). Testing checks if the product works properly (finding bugs). Evaluation determines whether it meets users' needs (usability). Together they improve the product before release. A school portal can be "bug-free" (testing passed) and still unusable if students cannot find the date sheet (evaluation failed). You need both. 1.11.1 Evaluation methods Worked example: when to use each method on a school portal. Week 2 of building: show the Lo-Fi to five students, change the menu. That is formative evaluation. A teacher who has studied HCI checks the screens against standard rules (Is feedback visible? Are labels consistent?). That is an expert review . After the portal is "finished", 30 students fill the 10 SUS questions. A low score means it is still hard to use, even if there are no crashes. Ask: "On a scale of 0–10, would you recommend this portal to a friend in another college?" That is NPS (loyalty). Compare the finished portal with the original goals (date sheet in one tap, bilingual fee notice). That is summative evaluation.
topics.speakUr: ٹیسٹنگ یہ دیکھتی ہے کہ پروڈکٹ ٹھیک چلتا ہے (بگز)؛ ایویلیوایشن یہ دیکھتی ہے کہ صارف کی ضرورت پوری ہوئی۔ SUS دس سوالوں والا استعمال کا اسکور ہے، NPS پوچھتا ہے کہ آپ یہ ایپ دوست کو کتنی تجویز کریں گے۔ فارمیٹو جانچ ترقی کے دوران ہوتی ہے، سمیٹو آخر میں اہداف کے خلاف۔ ماہر جائزہ ہیورسٹکس (Heuristics) پر ہوتا ہے۔

topics.speakEn: 1.11.2 Testing Methods (Usability, A/B, Automated). Testing involves observing how the system behaves under specific conditions. Learn all seven methods. The three named in the heading — usability, A/B and automated — are the ones examiners ask most, but a complete answer also names the others. Usability testing: observing real users while they perform realistic tasks, to measure efficiency and satisfaction. If the user gets stuck, designers know where to fix the UI. Task-based testing: assigning a specific task (for example, "Find a product and add it to cart") and strictly measuring completion time , success rate and number of errors . Automated audits: software bots scan websites to detect technical issues such as broken links, slow loading speeds or low colour contrast. A/B testing: comparing two versions of an interface (A and B). Half the users see A, half see B. The one with more clicks or sign-ups wins. Compatibility testing: verifying the system on different browsers (Chrome, Safari), devices (mobiles, tablets, PCs) and operating systems. Performance and load testing: simula
topics.speakUr: سات ٹیسٹنگ طریقے: یوزیبیلٹی (حقیقی صارف کو کام کرتے دیکھنا)، ٹاسک بیسڈ (وقت، کامیابی، غلطیاں ناپنا)، خودکار آڈٹ (بوت ٹوٹے لنک، سست رفتار، کم کنٹراسٹ ڈھونڈے)، اے/بی ٹیسٹ (آدھا صارف اے، آدھا بی؛ زیادہ کلک والا جیتے)، کمپیٹیبلٹی (براؤزر اور آلہ)، لوڈ ٹیسٹ (مثلاً دس ہزار لاگ اِن)، اور صرف کی بورڈ یا اسکرین ریڈر سے چل کر رسائی کی جانچ۔

topics.speakEn: Career Opportunities in UI/UX. The same HCI skills you practised on ATMs, JazzCash and school portals are real jobs. Each role uses a different slice of this chapter. Worked example: who does which JazzCash task? "Interview shopkeepers about sending money" → UX designer . "Pick the green, the typeface and the Send button in Figma" → UI designer . "On Tap Send, slide to Confirm, then Success" → interaction designer . "Run SUS and an A/B test of two Send buttons" → usability researcher . "Check contrast, captions and Tab order" → accessibility specialist .

topics.speakEn: 2.1 Analyze algorithms for correctness. An algorithm is correct if its output matches the expected results for a given input. Analysing correctness means showing that the algorithm produces the intended output for all valid inputs , not just one lucky example. Two methods are used in this course: Worked example: what “correct” means. An algorithm is supposed to count how many of the heights 1.91, 2.01, 1.87, 1.57, 1.48 lie between 1.57 m and 1.91 m inclusive. Expected output: 3 (1.91, 1.87 and 1.57 qualify; 2.01 is too tall; 1.48 is too short). If a program prints 4, it runs but it is not correct . Correctness is about the right answer, not about “no crash”.
topics.speakUr: الگورتھم تب درست (Correct) سمجھا جاتا ہے جب دیے گئے ان پٹ پر اس کا آؤٹ پٹ وہی ہو جو ہونا چاہیے۔ صرف چل جانا کافی نہیں؛ منطقی غلطی سے غلط جواب بھی نکل سکتا ہے۔ درستگی جانچنے کے دو طریقے ہیں: ٹریس ٹیبل (Trace Table) اور مرحلہ وار استدلال (Stepwise Reasoning)۔

topics.speakEn: 2.1.1 Trace Tables. A trace table is a technique used to monitor how the values of variables change during the execution of an algorithm. It is a paper execution of the code — a manual walkthrough, also called a dry run . You act as the computer and fill in one row after another. Purpose of trace tables Dry running: execute the algorithm line by line by hand. Debugging: find logical errors where the algorithm runs but the output is wrong. Validation: check that the algorithm does what it is intended to do. Components of a trace table Line / step number — which line is being executed. Variables — one column for every variable. Input / output — user inputs and printed results. Condition check — True/False for IF, WHILE, FOR, and similar tests. Worked example: soldiers who meet the height rule. To qualify for training, a soldier’s height must be between 1.57 and 1.91 metres, inclusive . Inputs: all soldiers’ heights. Output: the count of eligible soldiers. Step 1: Start Step 2: SET Total = 0 Step 3: Set AllHeights = [1.91, 2.01, 1.87, 1.57, 1.48] Step 4: FOR EACH height FROM AllHeights
topics.speakUr: ٹریس ٹیبل الگورتھم کا کاغذی اجرا (Dry Run) ہے۔ ہر قطار میں لکیر نمبر، متغیرات کی نئی قیمتیں، ان پٹ/آؤٹ پٹ اور شرط کا نتیجہ (True/False) لکھا جاتا ہے۔ فوجیوں کی مثال میں قد 1.57 سے 1.91 میٹر تک ہونا چاہیے، حدود سمیت؛ پانچ قدوں میں سے تین اہل ہیں اس لیے آؤٹ پٹ 3 ہے۔

topics.speakEn: 2.1.2 Stepwise Reasoning. Stepwise reasoning (also called logic verification ) breaks an algorithm into logical sections and checks the state of the algorithm at each stage. A state is a snapshot of what is true about the variables at that moment (for example, “Sum currently holds the total of the numbers seen so far”). You do not fill a row for every line. You think through the logic: Analyse each step of the algorithm. Check: does it start in a valid state ? Does it handle all possible cases ? Are the conditions correct ? If the loop is correct at the start of an iteration, does it remain correct at the end ? Worked example: sum of the numbers from 1 to N. Step 1: Start Step 2: Input N Step 3: SET Sum = 0 Step 4: For i = 1 to N Step 5: Sum = Sum + i Step 6: END For Step 7: Print Sum Step 8: End Stepwise reasoning breakdown Check What you verify Initial state Sum = 0 before the loop. Valid: nothing has been added yet. Loop boundary The loop runs exactly from i = 1 to i = N. No missing number, no extra number. Iteration Each i is added once: after k iterations, Sum = 1+2+…+k. Final s
topics.speakUr: مرحلہ وار استدلال میں الگورتھم کو منطقی حصوں میں توڑ کر ہر مرحلے پر اس کی حالت (State) دیکھی جاتی ہے: کیا شروع درست ہے، کیا تمام صورتیں سنبھلی ہیں، کیا شرط صحیح ہے، اور کیا لوپ کے ہر چکر کے بعد بھی نتیجہ درست رہتا ہے۔ ایک سے N تک جمع کی مثال میں Sum شروع میں 0 ہے، لوپ 1 سے N تک چلتا ہے، اور N=0 پر جواب 0 ہی رہتا ہے۔

topics.speakEn: 2.1.3 Comparing Trace Tables and Stepwise Reasoning. Both methods verify correctness, but they fit different situations depending on the complexity and length of the algorithm. Worked example: which method would you pick? A 12-line loop that adds five heights. Use a trace table . The loop is short, you are a beginner, and you need the exact Total. A billing system with 40 functions. Use stepwise reasoning . You cannot fill 10,000 rows. You check each module’s start state, end state and edge cases. A loop from i = 1 to 1,000 that should produce Sum = 500500. Do not write 1,000 rows. Argue: “Sum starts at 0; each i is added once; final Sum = n(n+1)/2 = 1000×1001/2 = 500500.” That is stepwise reasoning. Then dry-run a tiny N (say 5) with a trace table if you want extra confidence.
topics.speakUr: ٹریس ٹیبل خرد بینی (Micro) سطح پر کام کرتا ہے: ہر لائن اور ہر قیمت۔ مرحلہ وار استدلال بڑی (Macro) سطح پر ڈیزائن اور حالت چیک کرتا ہے۔ چھوٹے لوپ اور مبتدیوں کے لیے ٹیبل بہتر ہے؛ ہزار بار چلنے والے لوپ یا بڑے سسٹم کے لیے استدلال بہتر ہے۔

topics.speakEn: 2.2 Evaluating the Clarity of an Algorithm. Clarity means an algorithm is easy to read, understand and modify . In many cases, evaluating clarity is even more important than making the algorithm slightly faster. A clear algorithm is easier to maintain, debug and extend over time. The two key aspects of clarity are: Worked example: speed versus clarity. Algorithm A finds the class average in 8 confusing lines with variables a , b , c . Algorithm B uses two named functions and takes the same number of additions. Both are O(n). Algorithm B is the better school solution because the next person (or you, in three months) can change it without breaking it.
topics.speakUr: وضاحت (Clarity) کا مطلب ہے الگورتھم پڑھنا، سمجھنا اور بدلنا آسان ہو۔ بہت سی صورتوں میں وضاحت رفتار سے بھی اہم ہے۔ اس کے دو حصے ہیں: ماڈیولریٹی (Modularity) یعنی کام کو حصوں میں بانٹنا، اور پڑھائی پن (Readability) یعنی متن اور بہاؤ صاف ہونا۔

topics.speakEn: 2.2.1 Modularity. Modularity means breaking an algorithm into smaller, independent parts such as functions, classes or modules . This makes the algorithm more organised and easier to work with. How to evaluate modularity Single Responsibility Principle (SRP). Each module should focus on one specific task. If a function calculates a sum, prints a report and saves a file, it violates SRP. Coupling. Modules should be reusable in different contexts. Good modularity means loose coupling : a change in one part does not smash the others. Tight coupling is when two functions share so many hidden details that you cannot reuse one without the other. Abstraction. A well-designed algorithm hides complex implementation details. You can call a sorting function without knowing whether it uses Bubble Sort or Selection Sort inside. Worked example: average of an array. Poor modularity (monoblock) All logic sits in one block, so you cannot reuse the sum. Step 1: Start Step 2: Set A = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] Step 3: Set n = 5 Step 4: Set total = 0 Step 5: Set avg = 0 Step 6: For I = 1 to n Step 7: total = total
topics.speakUr: ماڈیولریٹی کا مطلب الگورتھم کو آزاد حصوں (فنکشن، کلاس، ماڈیول) میں توڑنا ہے۔ جانچ کے تین اصول: واحد ذمہ داری (SRP) یعنی ایک فنکشن ایک کام؛ ڈھیلی جڑت (Loose Coupling) تاکہ ایک حصہ بدلنے سے دوسرے نہ ٹوٹیں؛ اور تجرید (Abstraction) یعنی اندرونی تفصیل چھپا کر صرف کام منگوانا، جیسے سورٹ فنکشن بلائے بغیر یہ جانے کہ ببل ہے یا سلیکشن۔

topics.speakEn: 2.2.2 Readability. Readability is how easily another person can understand the purpose and logic of an algorithm without running it . It is about how clear the text and the flow are. How to evaluate readability Naming conventions — consistent rules for names. Good names make an algorithm easier to search and understand. Bad: v = d / t Good: velocity = distance / time Self-documentation — the algorithm explains itself, so you need fewer comments. Meaningful names and clean formatting make the purpose obvious. Control-flow simplicity — keep the logic straightforward. Avoid deep nesting (IF inside IF inside IF), limit extra conditions, and keep each function on one task. Consistency — one style throughout: indentation, spacing, and casing (camelCase or snake_case). Then the logic stands out instead of the mess. Worked example: the same formula, two styles. # Hard to read d = 100 t = 4 s = 20 v = d / t if v > s: if t > 0: print(v) 25.0 # Readable distance = 100 time = 4 velocity = distance / time speed_limit = 20 if time > 0 and velocity > speed_limit: print(velocity) 25.0 The second ver
topics.speakUr: پڑھائی پن یہ ہے کہ دوسرا شخص الگورتھم چلائے بغیر اس کا مقصد سمجھ لے۔ اچھے نام ( velocity = distance / time )، خود بیان (کم تبصرے)، سادہ کنٹرول فلو (گہری IF کے بغیر) اور ایک جیسا انداز (indentation اور casing) اسے آسان بناتے ہیں۔

topics.titleUr: کارکردگی (Efficiency) وقت (رفتار) اور جگہ (میموری) سے ناپی جاتی ہے۔ تی…
topics.speakEn: 2.3 Assess Algorithm Efficiency. Algorithm efficiency is measured in terms of time and space — how fast it runs and how much memory it uses. The key considerations for assessing efficiency are: Number of steps (described with Big O notation ). Number of conditions (IF decisions). Number of repetitions (loops). Worked example: two ways to find a name in 1,000,000 sorted records. Linear search checks about 1,000,000 names in the worst case (time grows with n). Binary search checks about 20 names (it halves the list each time). Both can be correct and clear. They are not equally efficient.
topics.speakUr: کارکردگی (Efficiency) وقت (رفتار) اور جگہ (میموری) سے ناپی جاتی ہے۔ تین چیزیں دیکھی جاتی ہیں: قدموں کی تعداد (بگ او)، شرطوں کی تعداد، اور دہرائی (لوپ) کی تعداد۔ چھوٹے ان پٹ پر تیز لگنے والا الگورتھم بڑے ان پٹ پر سست پڑ سکتا ہے۔

topics.titleUr: بگ او (Big O) بتاتا ہے کہ ان پٹ n بڑھنے پر وقت یا میموری کیسے بڑھتی ہے…
topics.speakEn: 2.3.1 Number of Steps (Big O Notation). When we discuss efficiency we ask how performance changes as the input size n increases. Big O notation is a mathematical method used to describe how the running time (or memory) grows as n grows. We ignore small constants and keep the most important term: if an algorithm does 3n + 5 steps we write O(n). In computer science, log n almost always means log base 2 (how many times you can halve n until you reach 1). Worked example A — O(1): first element of an array. Whether the array holds 10 or 10 million values, arr[0] is one jump to a known address. arr = [23, 76, 12, 90, 34, 68] print(arr[0]) 23 Worked example B — O(n): linear search. Each extra item adds one extra check. def linear_search(items, key): for i, value in enumerate(items): if value == key: return i return -1 print(linear_search([10, 50, 20, 70, 90, 30], 20)) print(linear_search([10, 50, 20, 70, 90, 30], 99)) 2 -1 Worked example C — O(log n): binary search on a sorted list. Each step throws away half of the remaining items. For 8 sorted numbers the worst case is about 4 comparisons
topics.speakUr: بگ او (Big O) بتاتا ہے کہ ان پٹ n بڑھنے پر وقت یا میموری کیسے بڑھتی ہے۔ O(1) مستقل (ایرے کا arr[0])، O(log n) ہر قدم پر آدھا (بائنری سرچ)، O(n) لکیری (لینیئر سرچ)، O(n log n) اچھے سارٹ جیسے مرج سارٹ، اور O(n²) مربع (ببل سارٹ، اندرونی لوپ)۔ بڑے n پر O(n²) ناقابلِ استعمال ہو جاتا ہے۔

topics.titleUr: ہر IF پروسیسر سے True/False پوچھتی ہے اس لیے زیادہ شاخیں کارکردگی گھٹا…
topics.speakEn: 2.3.2 Number of Conditions. Conditions (IF statements) are decision points. Every condition forces the CPU to evaluate True or False, so excessive branching reduces performance. Computational cost. Each IF is extra work, even if the rest of the algorithm is simple. Nested conditions. IF inside IF often means a brute-force approach. It hurts both readability and speed. Short-circuiting (the optimisation goal). Stop evaluating as soon as the result is known. In a logical AND, if the first part is False the second part is skipped. In a logical OR, if the first part is True the second part is skipped. Worked example: cheap test first. You only divide if the denominator is not zero. Place the cheap, safe test on the left so Python never evaluates the dangerous part. x = 0 y = 10 if x != 0 and (y / x) > 2: print("ratio is large") else: print("skipped safely") skipped safely x != 0 is False, so AND short-circuits and y / x is never attempted. If you wrote the division first, the program would crash. Same idea in the soldier algorithm: a False height test skips Step 6.
topics.speakUr: ہر IF پروسیسر سے True/False پوچھتی ہے اس لیے زیادہ شاخیں کارکردگی گھٹاتی ہیں۔ اندرونی IF اکثر brute-force ہوتی ہے۔ شارٹ سرکٹ (Short-circuit) کا مطلب ہے جیسے ہی جواب معلوم ہو جانچ روک دی جائے، مثلاً AND میں پہلی شرط False ہو تو دوسری نہ چلے۔

topics.titleUr: دہرائی (لوپ) کارکردگی کا سب سے بڑا عامل ہے۔ ایک بار ہر عنصر پر چلنے وا…
topics.speakEn: 2.3.3 Number of Repetitions. Repetitions (loops) are the most significant factor in algorithm efficiency. The structure of the loop decides how time grows with n. Worked example: count the inner-body runs. n = 5 linear = 0 for i in range(n): linear = linear + 1 nested = 0 for i in range(n): for j in range(n): nested = nested + 1 print(linear, nested) 5 25 One loop: 5. Nested loops: 25 = 5². For n = 1,000 that would be 1,000 versus 1,000,000.
topics.speakUr: دہرائی (لوپ) کارکردگی کا سب سے بڑا عامل ہے۔ ایک بار ہر عنصر پر چلنے والا لوپ O(n) (اچھا)، ہر بار مسئلہ آدھا کرنے والا O(log n) (بہترین)، اور اندرونی لوپ O(n²) (خراب) ہے۔ اندرونی جسم کے چلنے کی گنتی سے یہ فرق صاف نظر آتا ہے۔

topics.titleUr: کارکردگی کے تین سوال: کیا الگورتھم بڑے n پر چل سکتا ہے (Scale)؟ سب سے …
topics.speakEn: 2.3.4 The Efficiency Evaluation Framework. To evaluate an algorithm at a conceptual level, ask three questions: Does it scale? If n grows 10 times, does time jump 10 times (linear) or 100 times (quadratic)? Quadratic scaling fails for large datasets. What is the bottleneck? Focus on the most time-consuming section (usually the deepest loop) and try to improve that part. Is the cost worth it? A theoretically faster O(log n) algorithm can be too complex to code and maintain. For a list of just 50 items, a simple O(n) linear search is practically better because it is simple. Worked example: 50 names versus 1 million names. Situation Scale Bottleneck Worth the cost? Choice 50 unsorted class names Tiny n A single linear scan Binary search needs a sort first, which is extra work and extra code Linear search O(n) 1,000,000 sorted account numbers, searched all day n × 10 compared with 100,000 is already huge; quadratic would be impossible The search loop Yes — binary search is standard and well understood Binary search O(log n)
topics.speakUr: کارکردگی کے تین سوال: کیا الگورتھم بڑے n پر چل سکتا ہے (Scale)؟ سب سے سست جگہ کون سی ہے (Bottleneck، عموماً گہرا لوپ)؟ کیا تیز تر طریقے کی پیچیدگی اس چھوٹے فائدے کے لائق ہے؟ پچاس ناموں کے لیے سادہ O(n) تلاش عملی طور پر بہتر ہو سکتی ہے۔

topics.titleEn: 2.4 Refinements to improve clarity and efficiency
topics.titleUr: وضاحت بہتر کرنے کے لیے معنی خیز نام، ماڈیول، درست indentation اور مختص…
topics.speakEn: 2.4 Refinements to improve clarity and efficiency. Improving an algorithm means reviewing it step by step: simplifying logic, removing redundant work, and picking smart data structures. A clear algorithm is easier to follow; an efficient one wastes fewer steps. 2.4.1 Refinements for clarity Use meaningful names. Replace vague variables with descriptive ones. Bad: a = b / c . Good: average = totalSum / totalItems . Break into modules. Divide a massive block into functions, for example separating CalculateSum() from the printing logic. Improve structure and indentation. Packed loops and IF statements confuse the reader. Spacing reduces mental effort. Add comments. Keep them short. Explain why something is done, not just what is happening, especially for tricky logic. 2.4.2 Refinements for efficiency Reduce unnecessary steps. In Bubble Sort, after the first pass the largest value has settled at the end. Ignore that sorted tail on the next pass by shrinking the inner loop, and you save comparisons. Use better algorithms. topics.speakUr: وضاحت بہتر کرنے کے لیے معنی خیز نام، ماڈیول، درست indentation اور مختصر تبصرے استعمال کریں۔ کارکردگی کے لیے فضول قدم ہٹائیں (ببل سارٹ میں ترتیب شدہ دم نظر انداز کریں)، بہتر الگورتھم چنیں (لینیئر کی جگہ بائنری سرچ)، لوپ کے اندر وہی حساب بار بار نہ کریں (Caching/Memoization)، اور مناسب ڈیٹا سٹرکچر رکھیں۔

topics.titleUr: ڈیٹا سٹرکچر ڈیٹا کو منظم طریقے سے رکھنے کا نظام ہے تاکہ الگورتھم اسے ج…
topics.speakEn: 2.5 Concept of Data Structure. A data structure is a systematic way of organising, storing and managing data so that an algorithm can access, modify and process it efficiently. Real-life analogy. Books on a shelf are arranged in a set order, so you can find a title quickly. Files in folders are grouped on purpose. Data structures do the same job inside computer memory. Worked example: classify each everyday picture. Students standing in a single assembly line → linear (each has one in front and one behind). A family tree of grandparents, parents and children → non-linear (one parent, several children). Roads linking Karachi, Hyderabad, Sukkur and Larkana in many ways → non-linear (a network).
topics.speakUr: ڈیٹا سٹرکچر ڈیٹا کو منظم طریقے سے رکھنے کا نظام ہے تاکہ الگورتھم اسے جلدی استعمال کر سکے۔ لکیری ڈھانچوں میں عناصر قطار میں ہوتے ہیں (ایرے، لنکڈ لسٹ، سٹیک، کیو)۔ غیر لکیری میں ایک عنصر کئی سے جڑ سکتا ہے (ٹری، گراف)۔ الماری کی کتابیں اور فولڈرز کی مثال یاد رکھیں۔

topics.titleUr: ایرے ایک جیسے عناصر کو میموری کے لگاتار بلاک میں رکھتا ہے۔ ہر عنصر کا …
topics.speakEn: 2.5.1 Linear Data Structures: Array. An array holds a collection of similar items (the same data type) placed next to each other in contiguous memory (one continuous block). Each item has a position number called an index , usually starting from 0 . Because the address of any cell can be calculated from the index, you can jump straight to it. That is direct access (also called random access), and it is O(1). Worked example: read by index. A = [23, 76, 12, 90, 34, 68] print(A[3]) print(A[0]) 90 23
topics.speakUr: ایرے ایک جیسے عناصر کو میموری کے لگاتار بلاک میں رکھتا ہے۔ ہر عنصر کا انڈیکس (عموماً 0 سے) ہوتا ہے جس سے براہِ راست رسائی O(1) میں مل جاتی ہے، جیسے A[3] = 90۔ درمیان میں نیا عنصر ڈالنے کے لیے دائیں طرف شفٹ کرنا پڑتا ہے جو سست ہے۔

topics.titleUr: لنکڈ لسٹ زنجیر کی طرح نوڈز پر مشتمل ہے جو میموری میں بکھرے ہو سکتے ہیں…
topics.speakEn: Linear Data Structures: Linked List. A linked list stores data as a chain. Unlike an array, the items are not one continuous block. Each separate piece is a node sitting somewhere in memory. Each node has two parts: the actual data ; a link (pointer) holding the memory address of the next node. The first node is pointed to by HEAD . The last node’s link is NULL (nowhere). To find an item you start at HEAD and follow links one by one — sequential access , O(n). Real-life example: browser history. Clicking Back follows the pointer to the previous page-node. Worked example: walk from HEAD to print every data field. nodes = [23, 76, 12, 90] for data in nodes: print(data, end=" -> ") print("NULL") 23 -> 76 -> 12 -> 90 -> NULL There is no nodes[2] jump in a real linked list. The loop above models following each link once. Inserting a new node between 76 and 12 only means changing two pointers — you do not shift the rest of a big block, which is why lists beat arrays for frequent insert/delete.
topics.speakUr: لنکڈ لسٹ زنجیر کی طرح نوڈز پر مشتمل ہے جو میموری میں بکھرے ہو سکتے ہیں۔ ہر نوڈ میں ڈیٹا اور اگلے نوڈ کا پتہ (Link) ہوتا ہے۔ پہلا نوڈ HEAD سے ملتا ہے، آخری کا لنک NULL ہوتا ہے۔ براؤزر کا Back بٹن پچھلے نوڈ کے پوائنٹر پر چلتا ہے۔ رسائی ترتیب وار ہے، انڈیکس سے چھلانگ نہیں۔

topics.titleUr: سٹیک LIFO پر چلتا ہے: جو سب سے بعد میں آیا وہ سب سے پہلے نکلے گا۔ اوپر…
topics.speakEn: Linear Data Structures: Stack. A stack is a linear data structure that works on the LIFO principle: Last-In, First-Out . The last element added is the first one removed. You cannot pull an item from the bottom or the middle. PUSH — add an item to the top . POP — remove the item from the top . A TOP pointer always names the current top item. Real-life example: Undo in a text editor. Every action is piled on the stack; Undo POPs the most recent action first. Worked example: PUSH / POP trace. Start with an empty stack. Then PUSH Data1, PUSH Data2, PUSH Data3, POP, POP. Step Operation Stack (bottom → top) TOP Popped value 0 (empty) [] none 1 PUSH Data1 [Data1] Data1 2 PUSH Data2 [Data1, Data2] Data2 3 PUSH Data3 [Data1, Data2, Data3] Data3 4 POP [Data1, Data2] Data2 Data3 5 POP [Data1] Data1 Data2 stack = [] stack.append("Data1") stack.append("Data2") stack.append("Data3") print("after 3 PUSHes:", stack) print("POP:", stack.pop()) print("POP:", stack.pop()) print("left:", stack) after 3 PUSHes: ['Data1', 'Data2', 'Data3'] POP: Data3 POP: Data2 left: ['Data1'] Python’s list.append is PUSH
topics.speakUr: سٹیک LIFO پر چلتا ہے: جو سب سے بعد میں آیا وہ سب سے پہلے نکلے گا۔ اوپر رکھنا PUSH، اوپر سے ہٹانا POP، اور TOP پوائنٹر موجودہ سب سے اوپر عنصر بتاتا ہے۔ انڈو (Undo) کی مثال: ہر عمل ڈھیر پر پڑتا ہے، انڈو سب سے تازہ عمل ہٹاتا ہے۔

topics.titleUr: کیو FIFO پر چلتی ہے: جو پہلے آیا وہ پہلے نکلے۔ پیچھے (Rear) شامل کرنا …
topics.speakEn: Linear Data Structures: Queue. A queue organises data on the FIFO principle: First-In, First-Out . Whoever arrives first is served first. Order truly matters. ENQUEUE — add an element at the Rear (back). DEQUEUE — remove an element from the Front . Real-life example: several documents sent to a printer. The printer prints the first document received, then the next. Worked example: ENQUEUE / DEQUEUE trace. Start empty. ENQUEUE 55, 76, 90, then ENQUEUE D, then DEQUEUE. Step Operation Queue (Front → Rear) Front Rear Removed 0 (empty) [] — — 1 ENQUEUE 55 [55] 55 55 2 ENQUEUE 76 [55, 76] 55 76 3 ENQUEUE 90 [55, 76, 90] 55 90 4 ENQUEUE D [55, 76, 90, D] 55 D 5 DEQUEUE [76, 90, D] 76 D 55 from collections import deque q = deque() q.append(55) q.append(76) q.append(90) q.append("D") print("after ENQUEUE D:", list(q)) print("DEQUEUE:", q.popleft()) print("left:", list(q)) after ENQUEUE D: [55, 76, 90, 'D'] DEQUEUE: 55 left: [76, 90, 'D'] append is ENQUEUE at the rear; popleft is DEQUEUE from the front. The first DEQUEUE is 55 (the oldest), never D.
topics.speakUr: کیو FIFO پر چلتی ہے: جو پہلے آیا وہ پہلے نکلے۔ پیچھے (Rear) شامل کرنا ENQUEUE، آگے (Front) سے ہٹانا DEQUEUE ہے۔ پرنٹر کی قطار: جو فائل پہلے بھیجی گئی وہ پہلے چھپے گی۔ پہلی DEQUEUE ہمیشہ سب سے پرانا عنصر نکالتی ہے۔

topics.titleUr: ٹری ڈیٹا کو درجہ بندی (Hierarchy) میں رکھتی ہے جو ایک جڑ (Root) سے پھو…
topics.speakEn: 2.5.2 Non-Linear Data Structures: Tree. A tree organises data in a hierarchy . Everything branches out from a single starting point called the root . It creates a strict one-to-many (parent–child) relationship. That is an excellent way to show how roles flow in an organisation. Real-life examples: a family tree (grandparents → parents → children) and folders inside folders on a drive. Worked example: name the relationships. Root: Principal. Children of the root: Administrative Head, Academic Dean. Children of Academic Dean: HOD Math, HOD CS. HOD CS has one parent (Academic Dean), not two — that is the tree rule. If HOD CS also reported sideways to Accounts as an equal link, the picture would become a graph .
topics.speakUr: ٹری ڈیٹا کو درجہ بندی (Hierarchy) میں رکھتی ہے جو ایک جڑ (Root) سے پھوٹتی ہے۔ تعلق والدین-بچہ (ایک سے کئی) ہوتا ہے، جیسے پرنسپل → ڈین → ایچ او ڈی، خاندانی شجرہ، یا فولڈر کے اندر فولڈر۔ دو جڑیں یا چکر ٹری کو گراف بنا دیتے ہیں۔

topics.titleUr: گراف لچکدار روابط کے لیے ہے: کوئی سخت درجہ بندی نہیں، کوئی بھی نوڈ کسی…
topics.speakEn: Non-Linear Data Structures: Graph. A graph organises data when things connect in a flexible, complex way. Unlike a tree, there is no strict hierarchy : any node can connect to any other node. Nodes (vertices) — the items (cities, people). Edges — the connections (roads, friendships). Examples: Facebook friends; GPS mapping (the fastest route between two cities). Worked example: Karachi – Hyderabad – Sukkur – Larkana. Cities are vertices. Roads are edges. You can travel Karachi → Hyderabad → Sukkur or Karachi → Larkana → Sukkur. There is no single “root city”. That is a graph, and GPS uses it to pick a fast route.
topics.speakUr: گراف لچکدار روابط کے لیے ہے: کوئی سخت درجہ بندی نہیں، کوئی بھی نوڈ کسی سے جڑ سکتا ہے۔ نوڈز (Vertices) چیزیں ہیں، کنارے (Edges) تعلق۔ فیس بک دوست اور GPS نقشہ کلاسیکی مثالیں ہیں۔ چکر (Cycle) اور کئی راستے گراف کو ٹری سے الگ کرتے ہیں۔

topics.titleUr: ہر ڈیٹا سٹرکچر پر پانچ عمل ہوتے ہیں: داخل کرنا (Insertion)، حذف کرنا (…
topics.speakEn: 2.5.3 Operations on Data Structures. Whatever the shape, you keep meeting the same five operations: Worked example: name the operation. “Print every song from the start of the playlist.” → Traversal . “Add a print job at the rear.” → Insertion (ENQUEUE). “Undo the last typing action.” → Deletion (POP). “Is roll number 87 in the list?” → Searching . “Arrange heights from shortest to tallest.” → Sorting .
topics.speakUr: ہر ڈیٹا سٹرکچر پر پانچ عمل ہوتے ہیں: داخل کرنا (Insertion)، حذف کرنا (Deletion)، ایک ایک کر کے گزرنا (Traversal)، تلاش (Searching) اور ترتیب (Sorting، صعودی یا نزولی)۔

topics.titleEn: 2.6 Identify data structures in problem scenarios
topics.titleUr: اگر ہر عنصر کا واضح اگلا/پچھلا ہے تو ڈھانچہ لکیری ہے؛ اگر شاخیں یا کئی…
topics.speakEn: 2.6 Identify data structures in problem scenarios. To pick a structure, first see how the data is organised. If each item has a clear “before and after”, it is linear . If it branches or connects to many items, it is non-linear . 2.6.1 Linear scenarios Storing student grades for a class → Array. You usually know how many students there are, and all grades are the same type. Indices give rapid lookup. Music playlist / browser history → Linked list. Every song knows what comes next. When one finishes, follow the pointer. Frequent insert/delete is cheap. Undo or Redo → Stack (LIFO). Each typing or formatting action is PUSHed. Undo POPs the most recent action. Printer task scheduling → Queue (FIFO). Documents print in the exact order they were received. First-come, first-served. 2.6.2 Non-linear scenarios Organisational chart of a college → Tree. Principal is the root, then deans, then HODs, then teachers. Clear parent–child links. GPS navigation and maps → Graph. Cities are nodes, roads are edges. No strict top-down hierarchy. Several routes can reach the same destination. Worked exampl

topics.speakEn: 2.7 Trace data retrieval in Array, List and Queue. Tracing data retrieval means following the step-by-step path of how an algorithm finds or accesses data. Array, linked list and queue are all linear, but the effort to find an item is very different because of how they are organised inside. Worked example: three retrievals compared for “get 20 / get 87 / get A”. Structure Target Path Can you jump? Array [10, 50, 20, …] 20 at index 2 Array[2] in one step, or scan 10, 50, 20 Yes, if the index is known Linked list 12→98→23→87→… 87 Must visit 12, 98, 23, then 87 No Queue A-B-C A (the only legal retrieval) DEQUEUE Front No — never the middle

topics.speakEn: Career Opportunities in Algorithms. The skills in this chapter — proving correctness, writing clear modules, judging Big O, and choosing data structures — are the daily tools of several computing careers.
